6240: Baptist history contains both Particular (Calvinist) and General (non-Calvinist) streams from the seventeenth century. In America, the Separate Baptist and revivalist traditions often held a modified view: universal atonement and free response alongside eternal security, a combination that is neither five-point Calvinist nor classical Arminian. Through much of the twentieth century this was the majority outlook in the Southern Baptist Convention. The resurgence of Calvinism among young Southern Baptists from the 1990s provoked a response: *Whosoever Will* (2010), the Traditional Statement (2012), and then the online ministry of Leighton Flowers, who popularised the name 'Provisionism' (late 2010s) to distinguish it from both Calvinism and Arminianism. Critics on both sides have charged it with Semi-Pelagianism, a charge its advocates reject.

6295:
Confessional Lutheranism teaches that salvation is entirely God's work: the fallen will is bound and cannot cooperate in conversion, and God's eternal election of his children is the sole cause of their salvation. Yet Lutherans deny that God predestines anyone to damnation. Christ died for all, God earnestly wills all to be saved, and grace offered through Word and sacraments is genuinely resistible: those who are lost perish by their own fault.

Lutherans refuse to reconcile these truths by logic (the so-called crux theologorum, 'why some and not others?'), insisting that the comfort of election is to be found only in Christ as he is offered in the means of grace, and that speculation about God's hidden will leads either to despair or to presumption.
6296: Augustinian friar, professor at Wittenberg, reformer
6297: Luther's 1525 reply to Erasmus argued that the human will is in bondage to sin and that God works all things by his immutable will, distinguishing God hidden from God preached. He later counselled troubled consciences not to speculate about predestination but to look to the wounds of Christ and their baptism.
6300: Luther's colleague wrote the first Protestant systematic theology and the Augsburg Confession (1530). In later editions of his *Loci* he spoke of the will as a cause in conversion alongside the Word and the Spirit, which led to the synergist controversy among his heirs.
6303: The 'second Martin' of Lutheranism was a principal author of the Formula of Concord (1577), whose Article XI defines eternal election as God's gracious choice of his children in Christ, rejects predestination to damnation, and directs believers to the revealed will of God in the gospel.
6306: His multivolume dogmatics defended the Formula's teaching in the American election controversy (Gnadenwahlstreit) of the 1870s–1880s, opposing the view that God elected in view of foreseen faith (intuitu fidei).
6310: Contemporary scholar who explains for modern readers how Luther and his heirs held together the bondage of the will, election and the pastoral use of the gospel.
6311: Luther's early theology was strongly Augustinian, and his debate with Erasmus (1524–1525) put free will at the centre of the Reformation. After his death Lutherans quarrelled over Melanchthon's later language about the will (the synergist controversy) and over predestination as Reformed theology sharpened its formulations. The Formula of Concord (1577), collected in the Book of Concord (1580), settled the matter for confessional Lutherans: monergism in conversion, single predestination to salvation, universal grace, and a refusal to explain why some are saved and not others. American Lutherans revisited the question in the election controversy of the 1880s, which split the Synodical Conference.
6312: 1. Bondage of the will: in spiritual matters fallen humans can only resist God; they contribute nothing to conversion.
6313: 2. Monergism: conversion and faith are worked solely by the Holy Spirit through the means of grace (the Word and the sacraments).
6314: 3. Single predestination: God has chosen his elect to salvation in Christ, and this election is a cause of their salvation; he has predestined no one to damnation.
6315: 4. Universal grace: Christ died for all, and God earnestly desires all to be saved; his call through the Word is sincere to every hearer.
6316: 5. Resistible grace: people can and do resist the Spirit's work; the cause of damnation lies wholly in the sinner's unbelief.
6317: 6. Crux theologorum: why some are converted and others not cannot be explained; believers find assurance in Christ, baptism and the gospel, not in God's hidden counsel.
6318: God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world: election is real, eternal and christocentric, and should be contemplated only in Christ.
6319: Election is the cause of salvation and gives comfort to believers in suffering.
6320: God earnestly wills all to be saved; this revealed will is to be taken at face value.
6321: Christ wanted to gather Jerusalem and they would not: grace is resistible, and unbelief is the sole cause of loss.
6322: No one can come unless drawn by the Father: conversion is God’s work alone.
6323: Faith comes through the Word: God works through means, which is where election is to be sought.
6324: God saves by the washing of regeneration: baptism is a means by which God gives new birth.
6325: Israel’s destruction is from itself, but its help is from God (as traditionally read in the Lutheran confessions).
6326: Scripture teaches both that salvation is entirely God's work and that damnation is entirely the sinner's fault; Lutheranism affirms both without reducing either to fit a logical system.
6327: Inferring reprobation from election is a logical step Scripture does not take; reason should be captive to the Word rather than completing its doctrines by syllogism.
6328: God's revealed will in the gospel, not his hidden will, is the place where sinners meet God, so election is preached as comfort to believers, not as a puzzle.
6329: The Formula of Concord represents the mature consensus of the Lutheran churches after decades of controversy, carefully avoiding both synergism and double predestination.
6330: The means of grace (preaching, baptism, the Supper) are God's instruments for giving faith, so assurance rests on objective promises rather than introspection.
6331: The Lutheran view is logically unstable: if God alone converts, and he wills all to be saved, why are not all converted? Either God's will is frustrated or he does not in fact will to convert all, which implies something like reprobation.

6333: Lutheranism declines to explain how God's sovereign election coheres with resistible grace; middle knowledge could offer exactly that explanation.
6334: Luther's bondage of the will overstates human inability; Scripture repeatedly commands people to choose, repent and believe.

6336: The Lutheran claim that believers may lose their faith and salvation sits uneasily with single predestination: if election is a cause of salvation, how can an elect person fall?
6337: Lutherans accept that the question cannot be answered by reason and regard that as the faithful position, since Scripture teaches both monergism and universal grace. They argue that Calvinism resolves the tension only by subordinating texts on God's universal will to a logical inference.
6338: Lutherans reply that non-resistance is not a contribution to salvation (the dead do not cooperate) and that grounding salvation in human response would undercut the comfort of election; they prefer paradox to synergism.
6339: Lutherans regard speculative models of God's knowledge as an attempt to peer into the hidden God, which Luther warned leads to terror or pride, and see no need to supplement the Word.

6343: Lutherans are basically Calvinists on predestination.
6344: Confessional Lutherans explicitly reject predestination to damnation and limited atonement and teach that grace is resistible.
6345: Lutherans believe baptism saves automatically regardless of faith.

6347: Directs anxious consciences away from introspection to Christ and the sacraments.
6348: Holds firmly to both sovereign grace and universal grace without rationalising either away.
6349: Produced a rich confessional and liturgical tradition.
6350: Critics on both sides find it logically unsatisfying.
6351: Debates over election caused painful divisions (e.g. the American election controversy).
6352: Its paradoxical stance can be hard to teach to lay people.
6353: Confessional Lutheran churches: Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod, Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod, many Lutheran churches in Africa and Asia
6354: Historic Lutheran orthodoxy: Chemnitz, Johann Gerhard
6355: Twentieth-century theologians: Francis Pieper, Hermann Sasse

6358:
Eastern Orthodoxy understands salvation as theosis: through the incarnation, death and resurrection of Christ, human beings are healed and drawn into participation in the life of God by grace. This is a lifelong process in the Church, through baptism, chrismation, the Eucharist, prayer and ascetic struggle. Salvation is synergistic: God's grace always takes the initiative and does the work, yet the free human person must cooperate, and God never overrides freedom.

Orthodoxy rejects inherited guilt: humans inherit the consequences of Adam's sin (mortality, corruption, a tendency to sin), often called ancestral sin, but not Adam's personal guilt. God foreknows but does not predetermine who will be saved; predestination is grounded in foreknowledge, and God wills all to be saved.
6360: Bishop of Alexandria, defender of Nicene faith
6361: His treatise on the incarnation explains salvation as God the Word assuming human nature to restore incorruption and the divine image, culminating in the classic formula that God became human so that humans might become divine (paraphrased).
6364: Defended the doctrine that Christ has two wills (divine and human) against Monothelitism, which became the dogma of the Third Council of Constantinople (681). His theology of the will grounds Orthodox synergy: the human will, healed in Christ, freely conforms to the divine will, and deification is the goal of creation.
6367: Monk and theologian at Mar Saba
6368: His summary of Greek patristic doctrine taught that God foreknows all things but does not predetermine free human acts, so that predestination follows foreknowledge and virtue and vice are in our power with God's help.
6370: Lossky's influential presentation of Eastern mystical theology introduced Western readers to apophaticism, the essence–energies distinction and theosis as the heart of Orthodox soteriology, and helped shape the neo-patristic revival.
6373: His doctoral study argued that the Greek fathers did not teach inherited guilt but saw humanity's inheritance from Adam as mortality and corruption, which in turn give rise to sin; he sharply contrasted this with Augustinian theology.
6374: Orthodox soteriology was never shaped by a Pelagian controversy as the West's was; the Greek fathers wrote against pagan fatalism, Gnostic determinism and Manichaean dualism, and so emphasised human freedom (autexousion). John Cassian, often regarded in the West as Semi-Pelagian, is venerated as a saint in the East. When Calvinism reached the Orthodox world through Patriarch Cyril Lucaris's confession (published 1629), Orthodox synods rejected it, most fully at the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) and in the Confession of Dositheus, which affirmed that predestination is according to foreknowledge. Twentieth-century émigré theologians (Lossky, Florovsky, Meyendorff, Schmemann) and Greek theologians (Romanides) restated these themes for Western audiences.
6375: 1. The goal of salvation is theosis: participation in the divine life (God's uncreated energies), not in the divine essence.
6376: 2. Ancestral sin: humans inherit mortality and corruption from Adam, which give rise to personal sin, but not Adam's guilt.
6377: 3. Synergy: God's grace initiates, accompanies and completes salvation, while the free human person cooperates; grace never coerces.
6378: 4. Predestination according to foreknowledge: God foreknows all things but does not predetermine anyone's salvation or damnation.
6379: 5. Christ died for all and God wills all to be saved; salvation is received in the Church through faith, baptism, the Eucharist and a life of repentance.
6380: 6. Salvation is a process (I have been saved, am being saved, will be saved), and believers can fall away.
6381: Believers become partakers of the divine nature: the scriptural basis for theosis.
6382: Work out your salvation, for God works in you: the classic text of synergy, with God’s action and human effort together.
6383: We are God’s co-workers (synergoi): human cooperation with God.
6384: Christ prays that believers may be one in the Father and the Son: union with God.
6385: Through one man death entered the world, and because of death (as many Greek fathers read eph’ hō) all sinned: inherited mortality leading to personal sin.
6386: Believers are transformed from glory to glory into the image of the Lord: progressive deification.
6387: Those whom God foreknew he predestined: predestination follows foreknowledge.
6388: One must be born of water and Spirit: baptism as the beginning of new life.
6389: Christ stands at the door and knocks: he does not force entry but awaits the free response.
6390: The New Testament presents salvation as transformation into Christ's likeness and participation in God, not only acquittal.
6391: The Greek fathers before and after Augustine (e.g. Irenaeus, Athanasius, the Cappadocians, John Chrysostom, Maximus) consistently teach free will and cooperation with grace, which reflects the apostolic tradition.
6392: Love cannot be coerced; a God who is love invites a free response rather than determining it, and freedom is part of the divine image.
